glosses: to backpedal
Pédaler dans le sens contraire au sens de marche.

examples.text: Quand on en a goûté on a peine à revenir aux anciens systèmes, les manettes et poignées de commande paraissent barbares et primitives et d’instincts on renverse le mouvement des jambes pour changer la multiplication et rétropédaler.

glosses: Pédaler en sens inverse pour reculer (faire marche arrière)

examples.text: Il convient de remarquer qu'il existe un cas où l'on peut "rétropédaler" efficacement, c'est avec un pédalo

(...) « rétropédaler » signifierait « pédaler pour aller vers l’arrière ». (....) cet exercice est tout bonnement impossible avec une bicyclette ordinaire, munie d’une roue libre. Il faudrait (...) un vélo à roue fixe, (...) ce vélo permet à ces sportifs (...) de faire du sur-place mais, (...) on n’a jamais vu un pistard reculer ! En théorie, cela ne serait pas tout à fait impossible : on peut imaginer qu’en « rétropédalant » vigoureusement avec un vélo à roue fixe, le vélo se déplace vers l’arrière avec une vitesse suffisante pour se maintenir en équilibre. Mais ce doit être un exercice bien périlleux (...)

glosses: Renoncer, faire machine arrière, opérer un revirement.

examples.text: Conscient que le Président n’aime guère qu’une tête dépasse, il commence à rétropédaler en douceur, se montre soudain modeste.
Le commun des mortels, devant cela, s’est exaspéré, au point où la compagnie a senti le besoin de rétropédaler en ajoutant une précision dans un deuxième communiqué un poil moins jargonneux: […].
Fin janvier, le ministre de l'Intérieur, Bruno Retailleau, a félicité le collectif, se disant "très proche" de son combat – avant de rétropédaler.

glosses: An abandonment, withdrawal from, or softening of a previously expressed opinion, policy, argument, etc.

examples.text: It is interesting to speculate on what combination of factors acted within the Bush administration to bring about the climb-down from its previous position.
His climb-down from the "hard, secular" image was mainly to widen his support base.
Hours before his climb down, the premier's own cabinet ministers had vigorously defended the curriculum.

glosses: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see climb, down.

examples.text: It took 2 hours to climb up, but 4 to climb down as our energy grew less and less.

glosses: To abandon, withdraw from, or soften a previously expressed opinion, argument, etc.

examples.text: But Ekeus said Iraq had climbed down in its confrontation with the UN.
No, but it may be a way for Clinton to climb down from a policy he seems increasingly to view as a no-win proposition.

If they are interested in climbing down from their oppositionism, Democrats ought to consult the Progressive Policy Institute, which has been critical of Bush, but which is developing a balanced, positive approach to the energy crisis.

glosses: Alternative spelling of backpedal.
To reverse (a vehicle) from a confined space.

examples.text: He backed out of the garage.

glosses: To withdraw from something one has agreed to do.

examples.text: She backed out of organizing the fund-raising.

The girl threw back her head and laughed merrily. "You poor young man," she cried; "put that way it does sound alarming." Then she grew serious again. "There's plenty of time for you to back out now if you like. Just call the waiter, and ask for my bill. We'll say good-bye, and the incident will finish."

glosses: To convince (someone) to withdraw from a challenge.

examples.text:
"I can back you out."
"How? Doin' what?" they asked.
"Crossing the canal on the pole."
"Shucks, you can't back me out," declared one of the boys, at which he darted across the swaying pole, and with a jump, landed safely across. Another boy went at it gingerly, and with the antics of a tight-rope walker, he managed to get to the other side. […]
"All right, Carlia," shouted the boys on the other bank. […]
Carlia placed her foot on the pole as if testing it. The other girls protested. She would fall in and drown.
"You dared us; now who's the coward," cried the boys.

glosses: To bet on someone losing.

examples.text:
1921, Henry Luttrell, Crockford's : Or Life in the West Sketch No. III
Whatever you throw is your chance. I called five for the main, which is the out chance, and threw seven to it, which is the in chance. If I throw five first, I lose, and if seven I win. You can back me in by betting the odds, or you can back me out, by taking the odds, the bank answers either way.
See also: sell short

glosses: To undo (a change).

examples.text: I had to back out the changes made to the computer when it became apparent that they had stopped it working properly.

glosses: To exit a mode or function.

examples.text: I chose that menu option by accident, so I pressed Escape to back out.

glosses: To draw from behind the back (a knife etc.) (as also bare back).

examples.text:
Anything 4 get bun, back it out see the paigons run
Can't believe that my door got spun, I just got nicked for a loaded gun
